new_statements.rule_in_words: Isanzu is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with contrastive vowel length; the only first-hand description says nothing whatever about word stress or accent, and the authors state their data were insufficient to characterise even the tone system. No stress position can be assigned.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors explicitly decline to generalise about tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (elicited Swadesh-list words and short sentences); tone marked on vowels of citation forms; no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Isanzu proper (isan1243; speakers' name Kiihanzu, Maho F31B 'Isanzu' dialect of Nilamba F31) from one 38-year-old male consultant recorded at Haydom (Manyara region). The Johnson 1923-26 material examined for context is Nilamba/Kiniramba (nila1242), which Johnson himself says is 'not so much akin' to Isanzu; nothing from it is attributed to Isanzu.

sources.note: Nothing about stress or accent (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|penult = 0 hits). Says Isanzu has '2 level tones (H, L)' (abstract, p. 4); p. 8: all 7 vowels bear H or L tone and can be lengthened, 'Our data was not sufficient to make any generalisations about nature and functions of tone'; p. 11: lengthening and tones not marked in the practical orthography. Based on 3 days of elicitation (16-18 Aug 2018) with one male consultant.

sources.citation: Masele, Balla F. Y. P. 2001. The linguistic history of SiSuumbwa, KiSukuma and KiNyamweezi in Bantu Zone F. PhD thesis, Memorial University of Newfoundland. 827 pp. Handle 20.500.14783/12830.
sources.note: Comparative phonology/lexicostatistics of Sukuma-Nyamwezi-Sumbwa with other zone-F lects (incl. 'KiniHaanzu = Isanzu') as comparison wordlist data; Glottolog types it a wordlist or less for Isanzu. a full-text search for stress/accent the (poor) scanned text for stress|accent|penult finds only a remark that penultimate syllables tend to lengthen their vowels in JinaKiiya (Sukuma) verbs; no Isanzu stress or tone statement found. scanned caveat: the language name is mangled (one hit 'KlnrHaanzu', about reflexes of PB *c).
Nothing on stress; states 'Isanzu distinguishes between high tone and low tone', sourced to Beletskiy & Diyammi 2019.

sources.note: NILAMBA (nila1242, F31), not Isanzu: Johnson says the Anisanzu are 'not so much akin' to the Aniramba (p. 167). The sounds section (p. 168) gives no stress rule; the only stress remark (pp. 172-173) lists words that 'differ as regards stress' from Swahili (mba not mbwa, mbuu not mbu, usiu not uso, mtue not mtwe, -pia not -pya), i.e. syllabification differences.
